question: On 6 February, the Commission recalled that the use of nuclear power was necessary ‘to decarbonise the energy system by 2040’1. While nuclear is supposed to guarantee greater European energy sovereignty, in October 2022 the Polish government chose the US firm Westinghouse to build three reactors, rather than the EDF group2, enabling the United States to strengthen its influence in eastern Europe and weaken the EU.

Another step in this aggressive trade war against European firms is a bill which could be adopted by the US Congress to penalise Framatome3 for an agreement it concluded with Rosatom before the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, and for which there is currently no alternative.

It would allow Westinghouse to prevent Framatome from accessing its fuel market in power plants in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic, even though Framatome’s customers have made clear that they do not want to switch from a Russian monopoly to a US monopoly4. 1.
Is the Commission supporting Framatome in this context?
What specific initiatives does it propose to defend the European nuclear industry against these attacks?

‘Commission presents recommendation for 2040 emissions reduction target to set the path to climate neutrality in 2050’, press release, Commission website, 6 February 2024. ‘Nucléaire, une faillite française: comment les États-Unis ont remporté le “dossier polonais”’, L’Express, 28 May 2023. OpexNews, 27 March 2024. ‘Nucléaire: une alliance entre Framatome et le russe Rosatom fait des étincelles’, Le Point, 21 March 2024.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2024) The Member States’ authorities are responsible for selecting contractors (companies or consortia) of public procurement contracts, including those concerning the construction of nuclear power plants, based on the EU Procurement Directives.

The EU and the United States (US) are parties to the World Trade Organization Government Procurement Agreement1 and the EU has not excluded the construction of nuclear reactors from the coverage of this agreement2. Therefore, US economic operators have secured access to the EU public procurement market for the construction of nuclear power plants.

Additionally, in the REPowerEU Plan3, the Commission has called for acceleration of efforts to diversify supply of nuclear fuel and nuclear-related materials. Therefore, the Commission has been also working closely with the respective Member States on reducing and ultimately avoiding dependency on a single supplier4. The Commission is not in a position to comment on press articles and posts on social media5.
1 Which obliges its signatories to grant economic operators from other signatories a right to participate in their
public procurement market on non-discriminatory terms.

2 Except for the delivery of nuclear reactors in procurements by the Ministries of Defence and Agencies for defence or security activities in Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Hungary, Malta, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland and Sweden. 3 https://eur-lex.
